notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • A disease is a condition that disturbs normal structure or function of the body.
  • Diseases may be infectious or non-infectious.
  • Infectious diseases are caused by pathogens.
  • Non-infectious diseases include genetic, nutritional, metabolic, degenerative and lifestyle-related disorders.
  • Prevention depends on understanding cause, route of transmission and risk factors.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Disease → Infectious or Non-Infectious

2. Pathogen
  • A pathogen is a disease-causing organism or infectious agent.
  • Major pathogen groups include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoa and helminths.
  • Some diseases are caused by prions.
3. Communicable Disease
  • Communicable diseases can spread directly or indirectly between hosts.
  • Transmission can occur through air, water, food, vectors, body fluids or contaminated objects.
  • Examples include tuberculosis, influenza, cholera and malaria.
4. Non-Communicable Disease
  • Non-communicable diseases do not spread from person to person as infections.
  • Examples include diabetes, hypertension, most cancers and genetic disorders.
  • Many result from interacting genetic, environmental and behavioural factors.
5. Infection
  • Infection occurs when a pathogen enters and multiplies in a host.
  • Infection does not always produce symptoms.
  • An infected person without symptoms may still transmit some diseases.
6. Incubation Period
  • Incubation period is the time between infection and appearance of symptoms.
  • It varies by disease.
  • Transmission may sometimes occur during incubation.
7. Vector-Borne Disease
  • Vector-borne diseases are transmitted by organisms such as mosquitoes, ticks, fleas or flies.
  • The vector carries the pathogen from one host to another.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vector → Carrier of Pathogen

8. Air-Borne / Respiratory Transmission

Diseases spread through respiratory droplets, aerosols or close respiratory contact include:

  • Influenza.
  • Tuberculosis.
  • Measles.
  • Chickenpox.
  • COVID-19.
9. Water-Borne Disease

Important examples include:

  • Cholera.
  • Typhoid.
  • Hepatitis A.
  • Hepatitis E.
  • Several diarrhoeal infections.
10. Food-Borne Disease

Food-borne infections or intoxications include:

  • Salmonellosis.
  • Botulism.
  • Staphylococcal food poisoning.
  • Some forms of hepatitis A.
  • Amoebiasis through contaminated food/water.
11. Bacterial Diseases — Important List

Major bacterial diseases include:

  • Tuberculosis.
  • Cholera.
  • Typhoid.
  • Diphtheria.
  • Tetanus.
  • Pertussis.
  • Plague.
  • Leprosy.
  • Gonorrhoea.
  • Syphilis.
  • Anthrax.
12. Tuberculosis
  • Tuberculosis is caused mainly by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • It commonly affects the lungs.
  • It can also affect bones, lymph nodes, brain and other organs.
  • It spreads mainly through airborne particles from an infectious pulmonary case.
📌 Must-Memorise

TB → Mycobacterium tuberculosis

13. Tuberculosis Symptoms

Common symptoms may include:

  • Persistent cough.
  • Fever.
  • Night sweats.
  • Weight loss.
  • Coughing blood in some cases.
14. Tuberculosis Vaccine
  • BCG vaccine provides protection especially against severe childhood forms of tuberculosis.
  • BCG stands for Bacillus Calmette-Guérin.
  • It is derived from attenuated Mycobacterium bovis.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

BCG → Tuberculosis

15. Robert Koch and TB
  • Robert Koch identified the tuberculosis bacillus in 1882.
  • He received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1905.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Robert Koch → TB Bacillus → 1882

16. MDR-TB
  • MDR-TB means multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
  • It is resistant at least to isoniazid and rifampicin, two major first-line anti-TB drugs.
  • Incomplete or inappropriate treatment contributes to drug resistance.
17. Cholera
  • Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae.
  • It spreads through contaminated water and food.
  • Severe watery diarrhoea can cause rapid dehydration.
  • ORS and appropriate medical treatment are critical.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cholera → Vibrio cholerae

18. Vibrio cholerae
  • Vibrio cholerae is comma-shaped.
  • It produces cholera toxin.
  • The toxin causes intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vibrio → Comma-Shaped Bacterium

19. Typhoid
  • Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi.
  • It spreads by the faeco-oral route.
  • Contaminated food and water are important sources.
  • Good sanitation and vaccination help prevent disease.
📌 Must-Memorise

Typhoid → Salmonella Typhi

20. Typhoid Diagnosis — Widal Test
  • Widal test is a traditional serological test associated with typhoid.
  • It detects antibodies against Salmonella antigens.
  • Its accuracy is limited and interpretation requires caution.
  • Culture-based and modern diagnostic methods are generally more definitive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Widal Test → Typhoid

21. Typhoid Mary
  • Mary Mallon was an asymptomatic carrier of Salmonella Typhi.
  • She became historically known as Typhoid Mary.
  • She demonstrated that symptom-free carriers can transmit infection.
22. Diphtheria
  • Diphtheria is caused by toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
  • It commonly affects the throat.
  • A thick pseudomembrane may form.
  • The toxin can damage the heart and nervous system.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diphtheria → Corynebacterium diphtheriae

23. Diphtheria Vaccine
  • Diphtheria vaccine is a toxoid vaccine.
  • It is included in combination childhood vaccines such as DPT-containing formulations.
24. Tetanus
  • Tetanus is caused by Clostridium tetani.
  • Spores enter through contaminated wounds.
  • The bacterium produces tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin.
  • Disease causes painful muscle spasms and rigidity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Tetanus → Clostridium tetani

25. Lockjaw
  • Tetanus is historically called lockjaw because jaw-muscle spasm may occur.
  • The disease is not transmitted directly from person to person.
26. Pertussis
  • Pertussis is also called whooping cough.
  • It is caused by Bordetella pertussis.
  • It spreads through respiratory droplets.
  • Vaccination is the major prevention method.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Whooping Cough → Bordetella pertussis

27. Plague
  • Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis.
  • Fleas associated with infected rodents are classic vectors.
  • Bubonic plague causes swollen lymph nodes called buboes.
  • Pneumonic plague can spread through respiratory droplets.
📌 Must-Memorise

Plague → Yersinia pestis → Rat Flea Link

28. Black Death
  • The Black Death of the fourteenth century was a devastating plague pandemic.
  • Yersinia pestis is the causative bacterium.
29. Leprosy
  • Leprosy is also called Hansen's disease.
  • It is caused mainly by Mycobacterium leprae.
  • It affects skin and peripheral nerves.
  • Early diagnosis and multidrug therapy can cure the disease.
📌 Must-Memorise

Leprosy → Mycobacterium leprae

30. Gerhard Armauer Hansen
  • Hansen identified the leprosy bacillus in 1873.
  • Leprosy is therefore called Hansen's disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hansen → Leprosy Bacillus

31. Anthrax
  • Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis.
  • It is a spore-forming bacterium.
  • It affects animals and can infect humans.
  • Forms include cutaneous, inhalational and gastrointestinal anthrax.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Anthrax → Bacillus anthracis

32. Syphilis
  • Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum.
  • It is mainly sexually transmitted.
  • Untreated disease can progress through several stages.
  • It can also be transmitted from mother to fetus.
📌 Must-Memorise

Syphilis → Treponema pallidum

33. Gonorrhoea
  • Gonorrhoea is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
  • It is a sexually transmitted bacterial infection.
  • Untreated infection can cause infertility and pelvic inflammatory disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Gonorrhoea → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

34. Viral Diseases — Important List

Major viral diseases include:

  • Influenza.
  • Measles.
  • Mumps.
  • Rubella.
  • Chickenpox.
  • Polio.
  • Rabies.
  • Dengue.
  • Chikungunya.
  • Hepatitis.
  • HIV/AIDS.
  • COVID-19.
  • Japanese encephalitis.
35. Influenza
  • Influenza is caused by influenza viruses.
  • It affects the respiratory system.
  • Fever, cough, body pain and fatigue are common.
  • Influenza viruses can undergo antigenic change.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Influenza → Viral Respiratory Disease

36. Measles
  • Measles is caused by measles virus.
  • It is highly contagious.
  • Symptoms include fever, cough, conjunctivitis and rash.
  • Vaccination is highly effective.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Measles → MMR Vaccine

37. Koplik Spots
  • Koplik spots are small whitish lesions inside the mouth.
  • They are classically associated with measles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Koplik Spots → Measles

38. Mumps
  • Mumps is caused by mumps virus.
  • It commonly causes swelling of the parotid salivary glands.
  • Vaccination is included in MMR.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mumps → Parotid Swelling

39. Rubella
  • Rubella is also called German measles.
  • It is caused by rubella virus.
  • Infection during early pregnancy can cause congenital rubella syndrome.
  • Vaccination is important before pregnancy.
40. Chickenpox
  • Chickenpox is caused by varicella-zoster virus.
  • It causes an itchy vesicular rash.
  • After infection, virus remains latent in nerve tissue.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chickenpox → Varicella-Zoster Virus

41. Shingles
  • Shingles or herpes zoster results from reactivation of varicella-zoster virus.
  • It causes a painful rash typically along a nerve distribution.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Chickenpox and shingles are caused by the same virus.

42. Poliomyelitis
  • Polio is caused by poliovirus.
  • It spreads mainly through the faeco-oral route.
  • Most infections are mild or asymptomatic.
  • In a small proportion, the virus damages motor neurons and can cause paralysis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Polio → Poliovirus → Faeco-Oral Route

43. Polio Vaccines
  • OPV stands for Oral Polio Vaccine.
  • IPV stands for Inactivated Polio Vaccine.
  • Jonas Salk developed the inactivated polio vaccine.
  • Albert Sabin developed the oral live attenuated vaccine.
📌 Must-Memorise

Salk → IPV

Sabin → OPV

44. Rabies
  • Rabies is caused by rabies virus.
  • It spreads through saliva of infected mammals, usually through bites.
  • Dogs are a major source of human rabies transmission in many regions.
  • Once clinical disease develops, rabies is almost always fatal.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rabies → Animal Bite → Virus

45. Hydrophobia
  • Hydrophobia, or fear/spasm triggered by attempts to drink water, is a classic feature of symptomatic rabies.
  • It results from painful pharyngeal spasms.
46. Louis Pasteur and Rabies
  • Louis Pasteur developed an early rabies vaccine.
  • In 1885, Joseph Meister was famously treated using Pasteur's rabies vaccination approach.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pasteur → Rabies Vaccine → 1885

47. Dengue
  • Dengue is caused by dengue virus.
  • It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
  • Aedes mosquitoes commonly bite during daytime.
  • Severe dengue can cause plasma leakage, bleeding and shock.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dengue → Aedes aegypti

48. Dengue Warning Facts
  • Platelet count may fall in dengue.
  • A low platelet count alone does not determine severity.
  • Haemoconcentration and signs of plasma leakage are important in severe disease.
49. Chikungunya
  • Chikungunya is caused by chikungunya virus.
  • It is transmitted mainly by Aedes mosquitoes.
  • Severe joint pain is a characteristic symptom.
  • Joint symptoms may persist for weeks or months.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chikungunya → Aedes → Joint Pain

50. Japanese Encephalitis
  • Japanese encephalitis is caused by Japanese encephalitis virus.
  • It is transmitted by mosquitoes, especially Culex species.
  • Pigs and water birds are important amplifying/reservoir hosts in transmission ecology.
  • Vaccination is available.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Japanese Encephalitis → Culex

51. Hepatitis
  • Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver.
  • Viral hepatitis types include A, B, C, D and E.
  • Transmission routes differ among types.
52. Hepatitis A
  • Hepatitis A spreads mainly by the faeco-oral route.
  • Contaminated food and water are common sources.
  • It usually does not cause chronic infection.
  • A vaccine is available.
53. Hepatitis B
  • Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids.
  • It can become chronic.
  • Chronic infection increases risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.
  • A vaccine is available.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hepatitis B → Blood/Body Fluids → Vaccine Available

54. Hepatitis C
  • Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood.
  • Chronic infection is common.
  • It can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer.
  • No vaccine is currently available.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hepatitis C → No vaccine.

55. Hepatitis D
  • Hepatitis D virus requires hepatitis B virus for its replication cycle.
  • It occurs only in people infected with HBV.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hepatitis D → Requires Hepatitis B

56. Hepatitis E
  • Hepatitis E spreads mainly through contaminated water.
  • It is usually acute.
  • Severe disease risk is higher during pregnancy in some settings.
57. HIV
  • HIV stands for Human Immunodeficiency Virus.
  • HIV is a retrovirus.
  • It primarily attacks CD4 T lymphocytes.
  • Untreated infection can lead to AIDS.
📌 Must-Memorise

HIV → Retrovirus → CD4 T Cells

58. AIDS
  • AIDS stands for Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome.
  • It is the advanced stage of untreated HIV infection.
  • Severe immune suppression permits opportunistic infections and cancers.
59. HIV Transmission

Major routes include:

  • Sexual transmission.
  • Contaminated blood.
  • Shared needles.
  • Mother-to-child transmission.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

HIV does not spread through:

Handshakes.

Hugging.

Sharing food.

Mosquito bites.

60. Retrovirus
  • Retroviruses use RNA as genetic material.
  • Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA information into DNA.
  • HIV is a retrovirus.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reverse Transcriptase → Retrovirus/HIV

61. COVID-19
  • COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2.
  • SARS-CoV-2 is a coronavirus.
  • It spreads mainly through respiratory particles.
  • Disease severity ranges from asymptomatic infection to severe respiratory and systemic illness.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

COVID-19 → SARS-CoV-2

62. Protozoan Diseases — Important List

Major protozoan diseases include:

  • Malaria.
  • Amoebiasis.
  • Kala-azar.
  • Sleeping sickness.
  • Giardiasis.
63. Malaria
  • Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites.
  • It is transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.
  • Parasites first multiply in liver and then infect red blood cells.
📌 Must-Memorise

Malaria → Plasmodium → Female Anopheles

64. Major Human Malaria Parasites

Important species include:

  • Plasmodium falciparum.
  • Plasmodium vivax.
  • Plasmodium malariae.
  • Plasmodium ovale.
  • Plasmodium knowlesi.
65. Plasmodium falciparum
  • P. falciparum causes the most severe form of malaria.
  • It can cause cerebral malaria and severe anaemia.
  • It is responsible for a large proportion of malaria deaths globally.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Most Severe Malaria → P. falciparum

66. Plasmodium vivax
  • P. vivax can form dormant liver stages called hypnozoites.
  • These can cause relapses after the initial infection.
67. Malaria Cycle — Human and Mosquito
  • Female Anopheles injects sporozoites.
  • Sporozoites enter liver cells.
  • Merozoites later infect RBCs.
  • Some parasites form gametocytes.
  • Mosquito ingests gametocytes during a blood meal.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Infective Stage to Humans → Sporozoite

68. Ronald Ross
  • Ronald Ross demonstrated the role of mosquitoes in malaria transmission.
  • He received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1902.
  • His key malaria research was carried out in India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ronald Ross → Malaria Transmission → Nobel 1902

69. Amoebiasis
  • Amoebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica.
  • It spreads through contaminated food and water.
  • It may cause dysentery with blood and mucus.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Amoebic Dysentery → Entamoeba histolytica

70. Kala-Azar
  • Kala-azar is visceral leishmaniasis.
  • It is caused by Leishmania donovani complex.
  • It is transmitted by sandflies.
  • It affects the spleen, liver and bone marrow.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kala-Azar → Leishmania → Sandfly

71. Sleeping Sickness
  • African sleeping sickness is caused by Trypanosoma brucei.
  • It is transmitted by tsetse flies.
  • It can affect the nervous system and sleep-wake cycle.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sleeping Sickness → Trypanosoma → Tsetse Fly

72. Giardiasis
  • Giardiasis is caused by Giardia duodenalis.
  • It spreads through contaminated water or food.
  • It can cause diarrhoea, abdominal cramps and malabsorption.
73. Helminthic Diseases

Important worm diseases include:

  • Ascariasis.
  • Filariasis.
  • Hookworm infection.
  • Taeniasis.
  • Schistosomiasis.
74. Ascariasis
  • Ascariasis is caused by Ascaris lumbricoides.
  • Infection occurs by ingestion of eggs from faecally contaminated food, soil or hands.
  • Adult worms live in the intestine.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ascariasis → Ascaris lumbricoides

75. Hookworm Disease
  • Important human hookworms include Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus.
  • Larvae penetrate skin, especially bare feet.
  • Adult worms feed on blood in the intestine.
  • Chronic infection can cause iron-deficiency anaemia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hookworm → Skin Entry → Anaemia

76. Filariasis
  • Lymphatic filariasis is commonly caused by Wuchereria bancrofti.
  • Mosquitoes transmit the larvae.
  • Chronic lymphatic obstruction can cause elephantiasis.
📌 Must-Memorise

Filariasis → Wuchereria bancrofti

77. Elephantiasis
  • Elephantiasis is severe swelling caused by chronic lymphatic obstruction.
  • It is associated with advanced lymphatic filariasis.
78. Taeniasis
  • Taeniasis is intestinal infection with adult Taenia tapeworms.
  • Taenia solium is the pork tapeworm.
  • Taenia saginata is the beef tapeworm.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

T. solium → Pork

T. saginata → Beef

79. Cysticercosis
  • Cysticercosis occurs when humans ingest Taenia solium eggs.
  • Larval cysts can develop in tissues.
  • Neurocysticercosis affects the brain and can cause seizures.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Eating undercooked pork → Taeniasis.

Ingesting T. solium eggs → Cysticercosis.

80. Fungal Diseases

Important fungal diseases include:

  • Ringworm.
  • Candidiasis.
  • Athlete's foot.
  • Aspergillosis.
81. Ringworm
  • Ringworm is a fungal skin infection.
  • It is caused by dermatophyte fungi.
  • It is not caused by a worm.
  • It often produces circular itchy lesions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ringworm → Fungus, Not Worm

82. Athlete's Foot
  • Athlete's foot is a dermatophyte infection of the feet.
  • It is also called tinea pedis.
  • Warm, moist conditions favour infection.
83. Candidiasis
  • Candidiasis is caused by Candida species, commonly Candida albicans.
  • Candida normally colonises some body sites.
  • Overgrowth can cause oral thrush or genital candidiasis.
84. Deficiency Diseases

Important nutritional deficiency diseases include:

  • Vitamin A deficiency → Night blindness.
  • Vitamin B1 deficiency → Beriberi.
  • Vitamin B3 deficiency → Pellagra.
  • Vitamin C deficiency → Scurvy.
  • Vitamin D deficiency → Rickets.
  • Iron deficiency → Anaemia.
  • Iodine deficiency → Goitre.
  • Protein-energy deficiency → Kwashiorkor/Marasmus.
85. Night Blindness
  • Night blindness is commonly associated with vitamin A deficiency.
  • Severe deficiency can progress to xerophthalmia.
86. Beriberi
  • Beriberi results from severe thiamine or vitamin B1 deficiency.
  • Dry beriberi primarily affects nerves.
  • Wet beriberi primarily affects the cardiovascular system.
87. Pellagra
  • Pellagra results from niacin deficiency.
  • Classic 3 Ds are dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pellagra → Vitamin B3 Deficiency

88. Scurvy
  • Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency.
  • Bleeding gums and poor wound healing are characteristic features.
89. Rickets
  • Rickets occurs in children due to defective bone mineralisation.
  • Vitamin D deficiency is a major cause.
  • Bowed legs may occur.
90. Anaemia
  • Anaemia means reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood.
  • Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional cause.
  • Folate and vitamin B12 deficiency can also cause anaemia.
91. Goitre
  • Goitre is enlargement of the thyroid gland.
  • Iodine deficiency is an important cause.
  • Not every goitre is caused by iodine deficiency.
92. Diabetes Mellitus
  • Diabetes mellitus is characterised by chronic elevated blood glucose.
  • It results from inadequate insulin production, impaired insulin action or both.
  • Major types are type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Diabetes Mellitus → High Blood Glucose

93. Type 1 Diabetes
  • Type 1 diabetes is mainly caused by autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells.
  • Insulin production becomes very low or absent.
  • Insulin treatment is required.
94. Type 2 Diabetes
  • Type 2 diabetes is characterised mainly by insulin resistance with progressive beta-cell dysfunction.
  • It is the most common form of diabetes.
  • Risk factors include genetics, excess body fat and physical inactivity.
95. Gestational Diabetes
  • Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy.
  • It usually resolves after delivery, but future type 2 diabetes risk is increased.
96. Insulin
  • Insulin is produced by beta cells of pancreatic islets.
  • It lowers blood glucose.
  • It promotes glucose uptake and storage.
97. Diabetes Insipidus
  • Diabetes insipidus is different from diabetes mellitus.
  • It involves impaired ADH action or production.
  • It causes excessive dilute urine and thirst.
  • Blood glucose is not the defining problem.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Diabetes mellitus → Insulin/glucose.

Diabetes insipidus → ADH/water balance.

98. Hypertension
  • Hypertension means persistently elevated arterial blood pressure.
  • It increases risk of stroke, heart disease and kidney damage.
  • It often produces no obvious symptoms.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hypertension → High Blood Pressure

99. Atherosclerosis
  • Atherosclerosis involves plaque formation within arteries.
  • Plaques contain lipids, inflammatory cells and fibrous tissue.
  • It can reduce blood flow and promote thrombosis.
100. Coronary Artery Disease
  • Coronary artery disease results from narrowing or blockage of coronary arteries.
  • Reduced blood flow causes myocardial ischaemia.
  • Complete blockage can cause myocardial infarction.
101. Myocardial Infarction
  • Myocardial infarction is commonly called heart attack.
  • It occurs when blood supply to part of heart muscle is severely reduced or blocked.
  • Cardiac muscle tissue can die.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Heart Attack → Myocardial Infarction

102. Angina
  • Angina is chest discomfort caused by temporary myocardial ischaemia.
  • It does not necessarily mean heart muscle has died.
  • It differs from myocardial infarction.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Angina → Ischaemia without necessarily permanent necrosis.

MI → Heart-muscle death.

103. Stroke
  • Stroke occurs when blood flow to part of the brain is interrupted or when a brain blood vessel ruptures.
  • Ischaemic stroke is caused by blockage.
  • Haemorrhagic stroke is caused by bleeding.
104. Cancer
  • Cancer is uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells.
  • Cancer results from accumulated genetic and epigenetic changes.
  • Some cancers remain local while others invade and metastasise.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cancer → Uncontrolled Cell Division

105. Benign Tumour
  • Benign tumours remain localised.
  • They generally do not invade distant tissues.
  • They can still cause problems depending on size and location.
106. Malignant Tumour
  • Malignant tumours invade surrounding tissues.
  • They can spread to distant organs.
  • Malignant tumours are cancers.
107. Metastasis
  • Metastasis is spread of cancer cells from the primary site to distant tissues.
  • Cancer cells may travel through blood or lymph.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Metastasis → Cancer Spread

108. Carcinogen
  • A carcinogen is an agent that increases cancer risk.
  • Examples include tobacco smoke, ionising radiation, ultraviolet radiation and certain chemicals.
109. Tobacco and Cancer
  • Tobacco use strongly increases risk of lung cancer.
  • It also causes cancers of mouth, throat, oesophagus, bladder and several other organs.
  • Tobacco is one of the largest preventable causes of cancer.
110. Oncogene
  • Oncogenes are genes that promote cell proliferation when abnormally activated.
  • They can arise from mutations in normal proto-oncogenes.
111. Tumour Suppressor Gene
  • Tumour suppressor genes normally restrain cell division or promote DNA repair/apoptosis.
  • Loss of tumour suppressor function contributes to cancer.
  • TP53 is a famous tumour suppressor gene.
112. Apoptosis
  • Apoptosis is programmed cell death.
  • It removes damaged or unnecessary cells.
  • Failure of apoptosis can contribute to cancer.
113. Cancer Treatment

Major treatment approaches include:

  • Surgery.
  • Radiotherapy.
  • Chemotherapy.
  • Targeted therapy.
  • Immunotherapy.
  • Hormonal therapy for selected cancers.
114. Leukaemia
  • Leukaemia is cancer of blood-forming tissues.
  • It causes abnormal proliferation of white-cell precursors.
  • Several different types exist.
115. Lymphoma
  • Lymphoma is cancer arising from lymphocytes.
  • Major groups include Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
116. Cervical Cancer
  • Persistent infection with high-risk HPV is a major cause of cervical cancer.
  • HPV vaccination and screening help prevent disease.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Cervical Cancer → High-Risk HPV

117. Hepatitis B and Liver Cancer
  • Chronic hepatitis B infection increases risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
  • HBV vaccination therefore indirectly prevents some liver cancers.
118. Obesity
  • Obesity is excessive body-fat accumulation that increases health risk.
  • It raises risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
  • Genetic, environmental and behavioural factors contribute.
119. BMI
  • BMI = body weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.
  • BMI is a screening measure, not a direct measurement of body fat.
120. Osteoporosis
  • Osteoporosis is characterised by reduced bone mass and increased fracture risk.
  • It is common in older adults.
  • Risk rises after menopause in women.
  • Calcium, vitamin D, exercise and hormones affect bone health.
121. Arthritis
  • Arthritis means inflammation or structural disease of joints.
  • Major types include osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.
122. Osteoarthritis
  • Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disorder.
  • Articular cartilage deteriorates.
  • Age, joint injury and mechanical stress are major risk factors.
123. Rheumatoid Arthritis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.
  • The immune system attacks joint tissues.
  • It can cause chronic inflammation and deformity.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Osteoarthritis → Degenerative.

Rheumatoid arthritis → Autoimmune.

124. Autoimmune Disease
  • Autoimmune diseases occur when the immune system attacks the body's own tissues.
  • Examples include rheumatoid arthritis, type 1 diabetes and systemic lupus erythematosus.
125. Allergy
  • Allergy is an exaggerated immune response to normally harmless substances.
  • Allergens include pollen, dust mites, foods and animal proteins.
  • Histamine contributes to many allergic symptoms.
126. Anaphylaxis
  • Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapid systemic allergic reaction.
  • It can cause airway swelling and dangerous blood-pressure fall.
  • It is a medical emergency.
127. Asthma
  • Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of airways.
  • Airways become hyperresponsive and narrow episodically.
  • Symptoms include wheezing, cough and breathlessness.
  • Allergens, exercise, infections and irritants may trigger attacks.
128. Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
  • COPD includes persistent airflow limitation, commonly due to chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
  • Tobacco smoking is a major risk factor.
  • Air pollution and occupational exposures also contribute.
129. Emphysema
  • Emphysema involves destruction of alveolar walls.
  • Gas-exchange surface area decreases.
  • It is strongly associated with long-term smoking.
130. Pneumonia
  • Pneumonia is infection or inflammation of lung tissue.
  • It can be caused by bacteria, viruses or fungi.
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common bacterial cause.
  • Alveoli may fill with inflammatory fluid.
131. Meningitis
  • Meningitis is inflammation of membranes surrounding brain and spinal cord.
  • It can be caused by bacteria, viruses or fungi.
  • Bacterial meningitis can be rapidly life-threatening.
132. Encephalitis
  • Encephalitis is inflammation of brain tissue.
  • Viral infections are common causes.
  • Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne example.
133. Alzheimer's Disease
  • Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder.
  • It is the most common cause of dementia.
  • Memory impairment is often an early feature.
  • Amyloid plaques and tau pathology are characteristic.
134. Parkinson's Disease
  • Parkinson's disease is a neurodegenerative disorder.
  • Loss of dopamine-producing neurons in substantia nigra is important.
  • Tremor, rigidity and slowness of movement are common.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Parkinson's → Dopamine Deficiency in Basal Ganglia Pathways

135. Epilepsy
  • Epilepsy is characterised by recurrent unprovoked seizures.
  • Seizures result from abnormal electrical activity in the brain.
  • Causes are varied.
136. Genetic Diseases

Important genetic disorders include:

  • Down syndrome.
  • Haemophilia.
  • Sickle-cell disease.
  • Thalassemia.
  • Colour blindness.
  • Turner syndrome.
  • Klinefelter syndrome.
137. Down Syndrome
  • Down syndrome is usually caused by trisomy 21.
  • It results from an extra copy of chromosome 21.
  • Developmental and characteristic physical features occur.
📌 Must-Memorise

Down Syndrome → Trisomy 21

138. Haemophilia
  • Haemophilia A is commonly due to factor VIII deficiency.
  • Haemophilia B is due to factor IX deficiency.
  • Both are usually X-linked recessive.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Haemophilia → X-Linked Recessive

139. Sickle-Cell Disease
  • Sickle-cell disease is caused by mutation in beta-globin gene.
  • It is inherited mainly as an autosomal recessive condition.
  • Abnormal haemoglobin S causes RBC sickling under low-oxygen conditions.
140. Thalassemia
  • Thalassemia involves reduced production of alpha or beta globin chains.
  • It can cause severe anaemia.
  • It is inherited genetically.
141. Colour Blindness
  • Red-green colour blindness is usually X-linked recessive.
  • It is more common in males.
142. Turner Syndrome
  • Turner syndrome commonly has karyotype 45,X.
  • It affects phenotypic females.
  • Short stature and gonadal dysgenesis are characteristic.
143. Klinefelter Syndrome
  • Klinefelter syndrome commonly has karyotype 47,XXY.
  • It affects phenotypic males.
  • Infertility and testicular dysfunction are common.
144. Immunity
  • Immunity is the body's ability to resist infection and harmful foreign substances.
  • Immunity can be innate or adaptive.
145. Innate Immunity
  • Innate immunity is present from birth.
  • It responds rapidly.
  • It is relatively non-specific.
  • Skin, mucus, phagocytes and complement participate.
146. Adaptive Immunity
  • Adaptive immunity is antigen-specific.
  • It involves B and T lymphocytes.
  • It generates immunological memory.
  • Vaccination uses adaptive immunity.
147. Antibody
  • Antibodies are immunoglobulin proteins produced by plasma cells.
  • They bind specific antigens.
  • Major classes include IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD.
148. IgG
  • IgG is the most abundant antibody class in blood.
  • It can cross the placenta.
  • It provides passive immunity to the fetus.
149. IgA
  • IgA is important in mucosal secretions.
  • It is abundant in colostrum and breast milk.
  • It protects mucosal surfaces.
150. IgM
  • IgM is usually the first antibody class produced in a primary immune response.
  • It is efficient at activating complement.
151. IgE
  • IgE is important in allergic reactions.
  • It also participates in defence against certain parasites.
152. Vaccination
  • Vaccination produces artificial active immunity.
  • It stimulates memory cells.
  • Vaccines prevent or reduce severity of specific infections.
153. Antiserum / Immunoglobulin
  • Ready-made antibodies provide passive immunity.
  • Protection is immediate but temporary.
  • Examples include rabies immunoglobulin and antivenom.

159. TNPSC Traps
  • Communicable disease is not the same as all disease.
  • TB is bacterial, not viral.
  • Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae.
  • Typhoid is caused by Salmonella Typhi.
  • Tetanus is bacterial and toxin-mediated.
  • Tetanus does not spread person to person.
  • Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis.
  • Leprosy is caused by Mycobacterium leprae.
  • Ringworm is fungal, not a worm disease.
  • Dengue is viral.
  • Malaria is protozoan, not viral.
  • Female Anopheles transmits malaria.
  • Aedes transmits dengue and chikungunya.
  • Culex is associated with Japanese encephalitis and some filarial transmission.
  • Kala-azar is transmitted by sandflies.
  • Sleeping sickness is transmitted by tsetse flies.
  • Polio spreads mainly by faeco-oral route.
  • Salk → IPV.
  • Sabin → OPV.
  • Hepatitis A and E are mainly faeco-oral.
  • Hepatitis B and C spread mainly through blood/body fluids.
  • Hepatitis C has no vaccine.
  • Hepatitis D requires HBV.
  • HIV is a retrovirus.
  • HIV targets CD4 cells.
  • HIV is not transmitted by mosquitoes.
  • Chickenpox and shingles are caused by the same virus.
  • ORS treats dehydration, not the infection itself.
  • Diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus are different.

  • Type 2 diabetes → insulin resistance.
  • Down syndrome → Trisomy 21.
  • Turner syndrome → 45,X.
  • Klinefelter syndrome → 47,XXY.
  • Haemophilia → X-linked recessive.
  • Sickle-cell disease → autosomal recessive.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis → autoimmune.
  • Osteoarthritis → degenerative.
  • Cancer → uncontrolled cell division.
  • Metastasis → spread of malignant cells.
  • HPV is strongly linked to cervical cancer.
  • HBV can increase liver-cancer risk.
